Section 2.2 of Lock⁵ turns to a single **quantitative** variable and asks two
questions: what **shape** does its distribution have, and where is its **center**?
A dotplot or histogram reveals the shape — **symmetric**, **skewed to the left**
(long tail of small values) or **skewed to the right** (long tail of large values) —
as well as how many peaks (modes) it has. The two workhorse measures of center are
the **mean** $\bar{x}$ (the balance point: add up the values and divide by $n$) and
the **median** $m$ (the value that splits the ordered data in half). Skewness and
**outliers** pull the mean toward the tail while leaving the median almost unmoved:
for a symmetric distribution mean ≈ median, for right-skewed data the mean is
larger, and for left-skewed data the mean is smaller. Because the median is
**resistant** to extremes it is the preferred center for skewed data (paired with
the IQR), while the mean (paired with the standard deviation) uses every value;
for bell-shaped data roughly 95% of values fall within two standard deviations of
the mean, $\bar{x} \pm 2s$. The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking
the Power of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 81–86). Skill Builders 2.54–2.60 read
shapes off the eight histograms of Figure 2.12; 2.61–2.64 draw dotplots with
prescribed shapes; 2.65–2.68 compute means, medians, and outliers; 2.69–2.72 drill
notation. Exercises 2.73–2.93 apply the ideas to real studies, and the tabs based
on Lock5 data files include a small executable EDA.


## Exercise 2.54

**Which histograms are skewed to the left?** *(Refers to histograms A–H in
Figure 2.12 on page 82.)*

- **A and H.** Histogram **A** peaks at the right edge (near 1.5–2.0) with a long
  tail stretching left toward 0; histogram **H** rises gradually from −7 to a peak
  near −1.5. In both, the long tail of small values points left — the signature of
  left skew.

## Exercise 2.55

**Which histograms are skewed to the right?**

- **F and G.** Histogram **F** peaks at 0–2 and trails off gradually all the way to
  14; histogram **G** has a sharp peak near 2.5–3 with a longer, thinner tail
  extending to the right. The long tail of large values points right in each.

## Exercise 2.56

**Which histograms are approximately symmetric?**

- **B, C, D, and E.** **B** and **C** are symmetric with a single central peak;
  **D** is bimodal but the two modes are balanced mirror images; **E** is
  symmetric with a wide, flat top. Note that symmetric does not require
  bell-shaped — D and E are symmetric without being bell-shaped.

## Exercise 2.57

**Which histograms are approximately symmetric and bell-shaped?**

- **B and C.** Each has a single central peak with tails falling off steadily and
  roughly equally on both sides — the classic mound shape. D (two modes) and E
  (flat-topped) are symmetric but not bell-shaped.

## Exercise 2.58

**For each of the four histograms A, B, C, and D, state whether the mean is likely
to be larger than the median, smaller than the median, or approximately equal to
the median.**

- **A: mean smaller than the median.** The long left tail pulls the mean down
  while the median stays with the bulk of the data.
- **B: approximately equal.** Symmetric and bell-shaped — no tail is longer.
- **C: approximately equal.** Also symmetric and bell-shaped.
- **D: approximately equal.** Bimodal, but symmetric, so the two sides balance and
  neither measure of center gets pulled.

## Exercise 2.59

**For each of the four histograms E, F, G, and H, state whether the mean is likely
to be larger than the median, smaller than the median, or approximately equal to
the median.**

- **E: approximately equal.** The histogram is symmetric.
- **F: mean larger.** The long right tail drags the mean above the median.
- **G: mean larger.** Mild right skew produces a smaller but real upward pull.
- **H: mean smaller.** The long left tail drags the mean below the median.

## Exercise 2.60

**Which of the distributions is likely to have the largest mean? The smallest
mean?**

- **Largest mean: C.** Its values are centered near 75–100 (spanning about −50 to
  200), far above the centers of all the others — A and B sit near 0–1, D near
  10–13, G near 2–3.
- **Smallest mean: H.** Every value in H is negative (between −7 and −1), so its
  mean (about −3) is below every other distribution's, including E's (about −1).

## Exercise 2.61

**Draw any dotplot to show a dataset that is clearly skewed to the left.**

- Cluster the dots densely at the high end and let a long, thin tail of dots trail
  off toward the small values. One illustrative dataset of 85 values:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Illustrative dotplot of data clearly skewed to the left
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

def _dotplot(vals, ax, color="#4c72b0", s=18):
    u, c = np.unique(vals, return_counts=True)
    for v, n in zip(u, c):
        ax.scatter([v] * n, np.arange(1, n + 1), s=s, color=color)
    ax.set_yticks([])

left = np.clip(np.round(15 - rng.exponential(2.6, 85)), 0, 15)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 2.2))
_dotplot(left, ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.63

**Draw any dotplot to show a dataset that is approximately symmetric but not
bell-shaped.**

- Symmetry only requires the two sides to balance — the shape need not be a single
  mound. A **bimodal** dotplot with two equal peaks works, as does a flat-topped
  one:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Illustrative dotplot of data that is symmetric and bimodal but not bell-shaped

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 2.2))
_dotplot(bimodal, ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.65

**Data: 8, 12, 3, 18, 15.** *(a)* Find the mean $\bar{x}$. *(b)* Find the median
$m$. *(c)* Indicate whether there appear to be any outliers.

```{python}
#| echo: false
d65 = np.array([8, 12, 3, 18, 15])
pd.DataFrame({"Value": [d65.mean(), np.median(d65)]},
             index=["Mean", "Median"]).round(2)
```

- **(a)** $\bar{x} = 56/5 = 11.2$.
- **(b)** Ordered: 3, 8, **12**, 15, 18, so $m = 12$.
- **(c)** No outliers — the five values all sit reasonably close together.

## Exercise 2.69

**Give the correct notation for the mean:** the average number of calories eaten
in one day is 2386 calories for a **sample** of 100 participants.

- $\bar{x} = 2386$ calories. The 100 participants are a sample, so the mean is a
  statistic and takes the sample notation $\bar{x}$.

## Exercise 2.70

**Give the correct notation for the mean:** the average number of text messages
sent in a day was 67, in a **sample** of US smartphone users ages 18–24.

- $\bar{x} = 67$ texts. Again a sample mean (survey of some users, not all), so
  the notation is $\bar{x}$.

## Exercise 2.71

**Give the correct notation for the mean:** the average number of yards per punt
for **all** punts in the National Football League is 41.5 yards.

- $\mu = 41.5$ yards. Every punt in the league is included, so this is a
  population mean and takes the Greek-letter notation $\mu$.

## Exercise 2.72

owned per household for **all** households in the US is 2.6.

- $\mu = 2.6$ television sets. The value describes the entire population of US

## Exercise 2.73

**Arsenic in Toenails.** Arsenic is toxic to humans, and people can be exposed to
it through contaminated drinking water, food, dust, and soil. Scientists measured
the level of arsenic (in mg/kg) in toenail clippings of eight people who lived
near a former arsenic mine in Great Britain:

0.8  1.9  2.7  3.4  3.9  7.1  11.9  26.0

**(a)** Do you expect the mean or the median of these toenail arsenic levels to be
larger? Why? **(b)** Calculate the mean and the median.

- **(a) The mean.** The values pile up between 0.8 and 3.9 with a long right tail
  (11.9 and especially 26.0), so the skewed right distribution pulls the mean
  above the median.
- **(b)**

```{python}
#| echo: false
ars = np.array([0.8, 1.9, 2.7, 3.4, 3.9, 7.1, 11.9, 26.0])
pd.DataFrame({"Value": [ars.mean(), np.median(ars)]},
             index=["Mean", "Median"]).round(3)
```

The mean (7.21) is nearly double the median (3.65) — the 26.0 alone contributes
more to the sum than the bottom four values combined:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Toenail arsenic levels with the mean and median marked
u, c = np.unique(ars, return_counts=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.2))
for v, n in zip(u, c):
    ax.scatter([v] * n, np.arange(1, n + 1), s=28, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(ars.mean(), color="#c44e52", label=f"mean = {ars.mean():.2f}")
ax.axvline(np.median(ars), color="#55a868", label=f"median = {np.median(ars):.2f}")
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("Arsenic level in mg per kg")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.74

**Fiber in the Diet.** The number of grams of fiber eaten in one day for a sample
of ten people:

10  11  11  14  15  17  21  24  28  115

**(a)** Find the mean and the median. **(b)** The value 115 appears to be an
obvious outlier — compute the mean and the median for the nine numbers with the
outlier excluded. **(c)** Comment on the effect of the outlier on the mean and on
the median.

```{python}
#| echo: false
fib = np.array([10, 11, 11, 14, 15, 17, 21, 24, 28, 115])
fib9 = fib[fib != 115]
pd.DataFrame({"Mean": [fib.mean(), fib9.mean()],
              "Median": [np.median(fib), np.median(fib9)]},
             index=["With outlier (n = 10)", "Without 115 (n = 9)"]).round(2)
```

- **(a)** $\bar{x} = 266/10 = 26.6$ grams and $m = (15 + 17)/2 = 16$ grams.
- **(b)** Without the outlier: $\bar{x} = 151/9 \approx 16.78$ grams and
  $m = 15$ grams (the middle of the nine ordered values).
- **(c)** Removing 115 **drops the mean by almost 10 grams** (26.6 → 16.78) but
  moves the median by only 1 gram (16 → 15). The outlier dominates the mean
  because every value enters it, while the median — which only needs the middle
  position — barely notices: the median is resistant, the mean is not.

## Exercise 2.75

**Online Cat Videos.** In Exercise 1.69 we met a study of watching cat videos and
mood. Participants were asked how many cats they currently own, and the authors
report **2.39** as the measure of center for this right-skewed distribution.

**(a)** Is this measure of center the mean number of cats or the median number of
cats? **(b)** Would we expect the mean number of cats to be greater than or less
than the median?

- **(a) The mean.** Number of cats is a count, so every value is a whole number.
  A median of whole-number data can only be a whole number or halfway between two
  of them (such as 2 or 2.5) — it can never be 2.39. A mean, computed by dividing
  a sum by $n$, can be any value, so 2.39 must be the mean.
- **(b)** The distribution is right-skewed (many people own 0–2 cats, a few own
  many), so we expect the **mean to be greater than the median** — the median
  would be below 2.39.

## Exercise 2.76

**Insect Weights.** Consider a dataset giving the adult weight of species of
insects. Most species weigh less than 5 grams, but a few weigh a great deal,
including the largest insect known: the Giant Weta from New Zealand, which can
weigh as much as 71 grams. Describe the shape of the distribution of weights of
insects. Is it symmetric or skewed? If skewed, which way? Which will be larger,
the mean or the median?

- **Strongly skewed to the right.** The great majority of species cluster below 5
  grams — values cannot go below zero — while a handful of very heavy species
  (ending with the 71-gram Giant Weta) stretch the tail far to the right.
- **The mean will be larger than the median**: the enormous right-tail values
  pull the mean up while leaving the median with the typical insects.

## Exercise 2.77

**Population of States in the US.** The dataset *USStates* has a great deal of
information about the 50 states, including population. Figure 2.13 shows a
histogram of the population, in millions, of the 50 states. **(a)** Do these
values represent a population or a sample? **(b)** Describe the shape of the
distribution: approximately symmetric, skewed right, skewed left, or none of
these? Any outliers? **(c)** Estimate the median population. **(d)** Estimate the
mean population.

- **(a) A population** — the data include *all* 50 states (there is no sampling of
  states).
- **(b) Skewed to the right, with outliers.** Most states are small (frequencies
  decline steadily from the 0–2 million bar) while a few enormous states stretch
  the tail out to 40 million. California (about 39.5 million) and Texas are clear
  outliers.
- **(c)** Half of the 50 states have fewer people, half more; the median sits in
  that dense low region, around **4–5 million**.
- **(d)** The mean is pulled above the median by the big states, to roughly
  **6–7 million**.

*Data:* `data/ch02/USStates.csv` (n = 50), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/USStates.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
us = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/USStates.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
sns.histplot(us["Population"], bins=np.arange(0, 42, 2), ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(us["Population"].mean(), color="#c44e52",
           label=f"mean = {us['Population'].mean():.2f}")
ax.axvline(us["Population"].median(), color="#55a868",
           label=f"median = {us['Population'].median():.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Population in millions")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The actual values land right in the estimated ranges: median 4.57 million, mean
6.50 million — and the gap between them is exactly what the right skew predicts.

## Exercise 2.78

**Is Language Biased toward Happiness?** A recent study rated the top 10,222
English words on how positive they feel (1 = least happy, 5 = neutral, 9 = most
happy). The rating distributions for all four media sources had approximately the
shape in Figure 2.14. **(a)** Describe the shape. **(b)** Which of 3.5, 5, 6.5,
7, 7.5, 8 is closest to the median? **(c)** Will the mean be smaller or larger
than that median?

- **(a) Skewed to the left.** The ratings peak near 7–8 and drop off sharply on
  the right, while a long tail of lower ratings stretches back toward 2.
- **(b) 7.5.** The median sits just left of the peak region, where the curve
  crosses 50% of the area — clearly between 7 and 8 rather than at 6.5.
- **(c) Smaller.** With the long left tail, the mean gets dragged below the
  median (the mirror image of the right-skewed cases).

## Exercise 2.79

**Life Expectancy.** Life expectancy for all the countries in the world ranges
from a low of 52.2 years (Sierra Leone) to a high of 84.7 years (Hong Kong).
Life expectancies are clustered at the high end, with about half of all countries
between about 74 and the maximum of 84.7; a few countries, such as Sierra Leone,
have a very low life expectancy. The full dataset is in *AllCountries*.
**(a)** What is the shape of the distribution? **(b)** Estimate the median.
**(c)** Will the mean be larger or smaller than the median?

- **(a) Skewed to the left.** The values cluster between 74 and 84.7 with a long
  tail of a few low-life-expectancy countries reaching down to 52.2.
- **(b)** Since about half the countries fall between 74 and 84.7, the median is
  about **74 years**.
- **(c) Smaller.** The low-end tail pulls the mean below the median.

*Data:* `data/ch02/AllCountries.csv` (n = 217 countries), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/AllCountries.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
ac = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/AllCountries.csv")
le = ac["LifeExpectancy"].dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
sns.histplot(le, bins=np.arange(50, 88, 2.5), ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(le.mean(), color="#c44e52", label=f"mean = {le.mean():.1f}")
ax.axvline(le.median(), color="#55a868", label=f"median = {le.median():.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Life expectancy in years")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The dataset confirms the estimates: median 74.3 years, mean 72.5 years — the
mean, as expected for left-skewed data, is smaller.

## Exercise 2.80

**Making Friends Online.** A survey conducted in March 2015 asked 1060 teens to
estimate, on average, the number of friends they had made online. While 43% had
not made any friends online, a small number of the teens had made many friends
online. **(a)** Do you expect the distribution of number of friends made online
to be symmetric, skewed to the right, or skewed to the left? **(b)** Two measures
of center for this distribution are 1 friend and 5.3 friends. Which is most
likely the mean and which the median? Explain.

- **(a) Skewed to the right.** The count cannot go below zero, 43% of the teens
  are pinned at exactly 0, most of the rest made only a few friends, and a small
  group made very many — a textbook long right tail.
- **(b) Median = 1 friend, mean = 5.3 friends.** The median only needs the middle
  of the ordered data: with 43% at zero, the median lands among the low counts at
  1. The mean, in contrast, is dragged upward by the few teens with huge numbers
  of online friends — more than five times the median. Whenever the mean is much
  larger than the median, right skew is the reason.

## Exercise 2.81

**How Far and How Fast Do Homing Pigeons Fly?** For the 2019 Midwest Classic
homing pigeon race we have the speed (in yards per minute) and the distance (in
miles) covered from the release point to the home loft for each of the 1412
pigeons that finished. Figure 2.15 shows histograms of both variables. The
numbers **409, 429, 575, and 632** are the means and medians of the two
variables. Match each number with the variable and the measure of center.

- **Distance (miles) is skewed to the left** — the histogram peaks around
  400–500 miles with a long tail of short distances down toward 100 — so its
  **mean (409) is smaller than its median (429)**.
- **Speed (yd/min) is skewed to the right** — most pigeons clustered near
  550–700 with a long tail of slower birds out to 1500 — so its **mean (632) is
  larger than its median (575)**.

*Data:* `data/ch02/HomingPigeons.csv` (n = 1412 finishing pigeons), from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/HomingPigeons.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
hp = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/HomingPigeons.csv")
hp[["Distance", "Speed"]].agg(["mean", "median"]).round(1)
```

The dataset reproduces all four printed numbers — and the direction of each
mean-vs-median gap matches the direction of the corresponding tail:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Race distance and speed for the 1412 finishing homing pigeons with mean and median marked
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 2.8))
for var, ax in zip(["Distance", "Speed"], axes):
    sns.histplot(hp[var], bins=24, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.axvline(hp[var].mean(), color="#c44e52", lw=1.5)
    ax.axvline(hp[var].median(), color="#55a868", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_xlabel(var)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Frequency")
axes[1].set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.82

**Subtle Language Changes Impact Conflict Resolution.** A study in Israel
examined whether phrasing statements in noun form (such as "I support the
division of Jerusalem") rather than verb form (such as "I support dividing
Jerusalem") might reduce anger. In the study, 129 Jewish Israeli college students
were **randomly assigned** to hear statements in either noun or verb form, and
indicated on a 1–6 scale how much anger they felt. The mean score for those
hearing statements in noun form was **3.21**; for verb form it was **3.67**.
**(a)** Give notation for the two means. **(b)** Find the difference in means
(noun minus verb) and give its notation. **(c)** Is this an experiment or an
observational study?

- **(a)** $\bar{x}_N = 3.21$ (noun form) and $\bar{x}_V = 3.67$ (verb form).
- **(b)** $\bar{x}_N - \bar{x}_V = 3.21 - 3.67 = -0.46$: hearing statements in
  noun form goes with anger scores 0.46 points lower, on average, on the 1–6
  scale.
- **(c) An experiment** — the form of the statements (noun vs verb) was actively
  imposed and **randomly assigned** by the researchers.

## Exercise 2.83

**Donating Blood to Grandma?** Several studies in mice indicate that young blood
may reverse brain aging. Old mice were **randomly assigned** to receive blood
plasma either from a young mouse or from another old mouse, and one study
measured exercise endurance via maximum treadmill runtime (minutes) in a
90-minute window (Table 2.23; the data are also in *YoungBlood*):

| Group | Minutes on treadmill |
|---|---|
| Young (n = 17) | 27 28 31 35 39 40 45 46 55 56 59 68 76 90 90 90 90 |
| Old (n = 13) | 19 21 22 25 28 29 29 31 36 42 50 51 68 |

**(a)** Calculate $\bar{x}_Y$. **(b)** Calculate $\bar{x}_O$. **(c)** Find the
difference $\bar{x}_Y - \bar{x}_O$ and interpret it. **(d)** Experiment or
observational study? **(e)** If the difference is significant, can we conclude
that young blood increases exercise endurance in old mice?

```{python}
#| echo: false
young = np.array([27, 28, 31, 35, 39, 40, 45, 46, 55, 56, 59, 68, 76, 90, 90, 90, 90])
old = np.array([19, 21, 22, 25, 28, 29, 29, 31, 36, 42, 50, 51, 68])
pd.DataFrame({"n": [len(young), len(old)],
              "Mean minutes": [young.mean(), old.mean()],
              "Median minutes": [np.median(young), np.median(old)]},
             index=["Young blood", "Old blood"]).round(2)
```

- **(a)** $\bar{x}_Y = 965/17 \approx 56.77$ minutes.
- **(b)** $\bar{x}_O = 451/13 \approx 34.69$ minutes.
- **(c)** $\bar{x}_Y - \bar{x}_O = 56.77 - 34.69 \approx 22.07$ minutes: mice
  receiving young blood ran, on average, about **22 minutes longer** on the
  treadmill within the 90-minute window.
- **(d) An experiment** — the plasma treatment was **randomly assigned**.
- **(e) Yes, for these mice.** Randomization balances everything else between the
  two groups, so a significant difference would support the causal conclusion
  that young blood increases exercise endurance in old mice. Whether it extends
  to humans is exactly what the just-beginning human studies will have to test.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Treadmill minutes for mice receiving young or old blood plasma
yb = pd.DataFrame({"Minutes": np.concatenate([young, old]),
                   "Group": ["Young blood"] * len(young) + ["Old blood"] * len(old)})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.4))
sns.stripplot(data=yb, x="Minutes", y="Group", ax=ax, hue="Group",
              palette=["#c44e52", "#4c72b0"], size=5, alpha=0.75, legend=False)
ax.set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.84

**Price Differentiating.** E-commerce websites alter results depending on the
device or browser used. At Home Depot, the average price of 20 items when
searching from a smartphone was **$230**, while the average price when searching
from a desktop was **$120**. **(a)** Give notation for the two mean prices.
**(b)** Find the difference in means and give its notation.

- **(a)** $\bar{x}_{phone} = \$230$ and $\bar{x}_{desktop} = \$120$.
- **(b)** $\bar{x}_{phone} - \bar{x}_{desktop} = 230 - 120 = \$110$: the same 20
  items cost \$110 more, on average, when searched from a smartphone.

## Exercise 2.85

**Does It Pay to Get a College Degree?** US 2009 earnings data give the median
weekly earnings of high school graduates with no college degree as **$626** and
of college graduates with a bachelor's degree as **$1025**. Give correct notation
for and find the difference in medians.

- With subscripts identifying the groups, the medians are
  $m_{HS} = \$626$ and $m_{BA} = \$1025$.
- Difference: $m_{BA} - m_{HS} = 1025 - 626 = \$399$ per week. (Subtracting in
  the other order gives $m_{HS} - m_{BA} = -\$399$ — the order must be stated
  along with the answer.) Bachelor's degree holders earned \$399 more per week,
  at the middle of each distribution.

## Exercise 2.86

**What Is the Average Household Size in Canada?** The 2016 Canadian Census shows
that the average household size in Canada is **2.4** people per household. Give
the correct notation for this value.

- $\mu = 2.4$ people. The census covers **all** Canadian households, so this is a
  population mean and takes the Greek-letter notation $\mu$ (a parameter), not
  the sample notation $\bar{x}$.

## Exercise 2.87

**Create a Dataset.** Give any set of five numbers satisfying the condition that:
**(a)** the mean is substantially less than the median; **(b)** the mean is
substantially more than the median; **(c)** the mean and the median are equal.

- The lever is skewness: a **low outlier** drags the mean below the median, a
  **high outlier** drags it above, and a **symmetric** set leaves them equal.

```{python}
#| echo: false
sets = {"Mean less than median": [-100, 3, 4, 5, 8],
        "Mean more than median": [1, 2, 3, 4, 100],
        "Mean equals median": [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]}
pd.DataFrame({k: {"Data": str(v), "Mean": np.mean(v), "Median": np.median(v)}
              for k, v in sets.items()}).T
```

- **(a)** −100, 3, 4, 5, 8: mean −16 vs median 4.
- **(b)** 1, 2, 3, 4, 100: mean 22 vs median 3.
- **(c)** 2, 4, 6, 8, 10: mean = median = 6. (Any symmetric set works.)

## Exercise 2.88

**Describe a Variable.** Describe one quantitative variable that you believe will
give data that are skewed to the right, and explain your reasoning. Do not use a
variable already discussed.

- **Example: household income** (or: number of social media followers, length of
  hospital stays). Incomes cannot drop below zero, most households earn modest
  to moderate amounts, and a small number of very high earners stretch the tail
  out to the right — many values bunched low, a few extremely large ones, hence
  right skew.

## Exercise 2.89

**Distribution of Birth Rate.** The *BirthRate* variable in the *AllCountries*
dataset gives the birth rate per 1000 people for all the countries in the world.
Use technology to create a histogram, and describe the shape: relatively
symmetric, mildly skewed, or strongly skewed?

*Data:* `data/ch02/AllCountries.csv` (n = 217 countries), from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/AllCountries.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Birth rate per 1000 people for 217 countries with mean and median marked
br = ac["BirthRate"].dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
sns.histplot(br, bins=np.arange(6, 50, 2), ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(br.mean(), color="#c44e52", label=f"mean = {br.mean():.1f}")
ax.axvline(br.median(), color="#55a868", label=f"median = {br.median():.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Births per 1000 people")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **Strongly skewed to the right.** Most countries cluster between about 8 and
  25 births per 1000, and a long tail of high-birth-rate countries (up to about
  48) stretches far to the right. The mean (20.1) sits well above the median
  (17.9), confirming the strong right skew.

**Enrollments at Two-year Colleges.** The dataset *CollegeScores2yr* has
information on the number of students enrolled at each US college where the
primary degree is an Associate's degree. **(a)** Create a plot of the
*Enrollment* variable. What is the most striking feature of the shape? **(b)**
Find the mean and median. **(c)** Explain the connection between (a) and (b).

*Data:* `data/ch02/CollegeScores2yr.csv` (n = 1141 colleges with enrollment
reported), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CollegeScores2yr.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
c2 = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/CollegeScores2yr.csv")

pd.DataFrame({"Value": [enr2.mean(), enr2.median(), enr2.max()]},
             index=["Mean enrollment", "Median enrollment",
                    "Largest college"]).round(0).astype(int)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Enrollment at 1141 two-year colleges with mean and median marked
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
sns.histplot(enr2, bins=60, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(enr2.mean(), color="#c44e52", label=f"mean = {enr2.mean():.0f}")
```

- **(a)** The most striking feature is the **extreme right skew with a handful of
  enormous outliers**: the median college enrolls under 2000 students, but a few
  huge community college systems top 50,000 (Lone Star College System at 59,107,
  Houston Community College, Miami Dade College).
- **(b)** Mean ≈ **4050** students; median ≈ **1748** students.
- **(c)** The strong right skew is exactly why the mean is more than double the
  median: the few giant campuses contribute enormously to the sum (and hence the
  mean) but do not move the median at all.

## Exercise 2.93

**Number of Children.** Table 2.24 shows the number of women (per 1000) between
ages 15 and 50 who have been married, grouped by number of children; Table 2.25
gives the same information for women who have never been married.

| Number of children | Ever married | Never married |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 162 | 752 |
| 1 | 213 | 117 |
| 2 | 344 | 72 |
| 3 | 182 | 35 |
| 4 | 69 | 15 |
| 5+ | 32 | 10 |

**(a)** Without doing any calculations, which of the two samples appears to have
the highest mean number of children? Which distribution appears to have the mean
most different from the median? Why? **(b)** Find the median for each dataset.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Number of children per 1000 women who have or have never been married
kids = pd.DataFrame({"Children": [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
                     "Ever married": [162, 213, 344, 182, 69, 32],
                     "Never married": [752, 117, 72, 35, 15, 10]})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3))
kids.plot.bar(x="Children", y=["Ever married", "Never married"], ax=ax,
              rot=0, color=["#4c72b0", "#c44e52"], width=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Number of children")
ax.set_ylabel("Women per 1000")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **(a) Highest mean: the ever-married sample.** Its counts center on 2–3
  children, while the never-married counts pile up overwhelmingly at zero.
  **Mean most different from median: the never-married sample.** That
  distribution is extremely right-skewed — 752 of 1000 women have no children,
  with a long thin tail out to 5 — so the few large values pull the mean well
  above the median, which stays at zero. The ever-married distribution is much
  more nearly symmetric, so its mean and median nearly coincide. (Treating
  "5+" as 5:)

```{python}
#| echo: false
stats = {}
for grp in ["Ever married", "Never married"]:
    rep = np.repeat(kids["Children"].to_numpy(), kids[grp].to_numpy())
    stats[grp] = {"Mean children": np.average(kids["Children"],
                                              weights=kids[grp]),
                  "Median children": np.median(rep)}
pd.DataFrame(stats).T.round(2)
```

- **(b)** **Ever married: median = 2 children** (the 500th of the 1000 women
  falls in the two-children group). **Never married: median = 0 children** (752
  of the 1000 have none, so the median lands inside the zero group).

:::
